The Mozambique large-eye bream Wattsia mossambica, a member of the Lethrinidae family, exhibits life-history traits characteristic of a relatively slow-growing, late-maturing teleost. Field maturation studies, primarily conducted using trawl surveys along the East African coast, indicate that the onset of gonad recrudescence and gametogenesis occurs at a total length of 31 cm [Lp = 31 cm], a size that typically corresponds to several years of post-settlement growth. This length at puberty represents a significant proportion of the species' ultimate total length, which has been recorded at 55 cm [Li = 55 cm] in the largest individual captured during long-term reef monitoring programs. Comparative studies with related species, such as those from the genus Lethrinus, suggest that this pattern of delayed maturation is linked to the energetic demands of reaching the body size required to exploit larger, more nutritious benthic prey. The body mass at which these fish attain puberty has been estimated from length-weight regressions to be approximately 483 grams [Wwp = approximately 483 grams].

Examining the earliest life stages, the initial body mass of the newly emerged yolk-sac larva is exceptionally small, reflecting a high fecundity strategy. Based on an egg diameter of 0.335 mm, the calculated wet weight at birth is 0.00002 grams [Wwb = 0.00002 grams], placing the embryo firmly within the range of pelagic-spawning teleosts that produce large numbers of small, buoyant eggs. This minimal starting mass necessitates a rapid development phase: the yolk-dependent alevin stage is brief, with the chorion rupture occurring within a few days post-fertilization in waters of 19.9 °C [T = 19.9 °C]. The transition to exogenous feeding is a critical bottleneck, as the tiny mouth gape limits initial prey size to small copepod nauplii. This vulnerability is offset by the sheer number of offspring produced, a classic feature of the species' reproductive strategy.

Reproductive output in Wattsia mossambica is substantial, a necessity given the high mortality rates experienced during the planktonic larval phase. Data extrapolated from congeneric species suggest that a mature female produces approximately 493 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 493 eggs per day] at 19.9 °C [T = 19.9 °C], with the species being an iteroparous adult capable of multiple spawning events in a single season. Observations of gravid fish and spawning aggregations on the outer reef slope indicate that this daily rate supports a steady annual reproductive output. These reproductive metrics are typical for a species inhabiting a stable but resource-limited coral reef ecosystem.

The asymptotic body mass of a fully grown individual provides further insight into the species' maximum energetic capacity. The ultimate wet weight for Wattsia mossambica, derived from the length-weight power function common to the Lethrinidae, is approximately 2640 grams [Wwi = approximately 2640 grams]. This figure represents the maximum recorded body mass in adults, typically achieved by the oldest and most dominant individuals in the population. Reaching this asymptotic size requires a prolonged period of accelerated growth followed by a plateau, a pattern confirmed by otolith increment analysis. This ultimate body mass is nearly five and a half times the weight at puberty, underscoring the significant post-maturation somatic investment that continues even after the fish becomes reproductively viable. Such a life-history strategy prioritizes long-term survival and competitive dominance in the reef environment.

A full appreciation of the life-history trade-offs in Wattsia mossambica requires consideration of its entire lifespan. Under the ambient thermal conditions of the western Indian Ocean, which average 19.9 °C [T = 19.9 °C], the maximum recorded longevity for this species has been estimated at 10 years [am = 10 years]. This lifespan, determined through analysis of annual growth zones in sagittal otoliths, places the species among the longer-lived members of its family. The decadal duration of life allows multiple reproductive cycles, reinforcing the species' iteroparous strategy. The interplay between a late age at first reproduction, a moderate annual reproductive output, and a lifespan of 10 years indicates a relatively stable population dynamic, well-suited to the predictable, albeit competitive, conditions of its coral reef habitat.
